title: Undo and Redo
statement: A tiny text editor starts empty and supports four commands:
`type <word>` appends the word, which is letters only, to the end of the text.
`delete <k>` removes the last k characters, or everything if there are fewer than k.
`undo` reverts the most recent `type` or `delete` that hasn't been undone yet, and does nothing if there isn't one.
`redo` re-applies the most recently undone change, and does nothing if there isn't one. Any new `type` or `delete` clears the changes available to redo.
Every `type` and `delete` counts as a change, even one that removes nothing. Return the text after running all the commands.

examples.explanation: The text goes hello, helloworld, hellowo, then undo twice back to hello, and redo brings back helloworld.
Typing x after the undo clears the redo history.

hints: What do you need to store about each change so you can reverse it later?
Keep two stacks: changes you can undo and changes you can redo. Undo moves the top change from one to the other.
For a delete, store the characters that were actually removed, so undo can put them back even when k was bigger than the text.
pitfalls: Storing k for a delete instead of the removed characters, which breaks undo when k was larger than the text.
Forgetting to clear the redo stack on a new type or delete.
Letting undo or redo crash when its stack is empty.
Saving a full copy of the text for every change, which works but uses far more memory.
interviewerNotes: Ask them to compare storing snapshots with storing the change itself.
Probe deleting more than the text holds, then undoing it.
Ask whether undoing a delete of 0 should count as an undo step, and check they read the statement.
Follow-ups: add a cursor that can move, or group consecutive typing into one undo step.
